claim: During eukaryotic evolution, genome size has increased disproportionately to nuclear volume.
source: During eukaryotic evolution, genome size has increased disproportionately to nuclear volume, necessitating greater degrees of chromatin compaction in higher eukaryotes, which have evolved several mechanisms for genome compaction.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on nuclear volume and genome size relationships.

claim: Higher eukaryotes require greater degrees of chromatin compaction than organisms with smaller genomes.
source: During eukaryotic evolution, genome size has increased disproportionately to nuclear volume, necessitating greater degrees of chromatin compaction in higher eukaryotes, which have evolved several mechanisms for genome compaction.
evidence: Logical inference from the disproportionate increase in genome size relative to nuclear volume.

claim: The H2A N-terminus has systematically acquired arginines as genomes expanded.
source: Analysis of histone sequences from 160 eukaryotes revealed that the H2A N-terminus has systematically acquired arginines as genomes expanded.
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of 160 eukaryotic histone sequences presented in the manuscript.

claim: Insertion of arginines into their evolutionarily conserved position in H2A of a small-genome organism increased linear compaction by as much as 40%.
source: Insertion of arginines into their evolutionarily conserved position in H2A of a small-genome organism increased linear compaction by as much as 40%, while their absence markedly diminished compaction in cells with large genomes.
evidence: Supported by FISH experiments in yeast cells showing decreased interprobe distances.

claim: Absence of H2A N-terminal arginines markedly diminished compaction in cells with large genomes.
source: Insertion of arginines into their evolutionarily conserved position in H2A of a small-genome organism increased linear compaction by as much as 40%, while their absence markedly diminished compaction in cells with large genomes.
evidence: Supported by experiments in human cells showing increased interprobe distances when arginines are removed.

claim: The H2A N-terminus directly modulates the chromatin fiber through intra- and inter-nucleosomal arginine–DNA contacts.
source: This effect was recapitulated in vitro with nucleosomal arrays using unmodified histones, indicating that the H2A N-terminus directly modulates the chromatin fiber likely through intra- and inter-nucleosomal arginine–DNA contacts to enable tighter nucleosomal packing.
evidence: Supported by in vitro analytical ultracentrifugation experiments with reconstituted nucleosomal arrays.

claim: The H2A N-terminus enables tighter nucleosomal packing through arginine-DNA contacts.
source: This effect was recapitulated in vitro with nucleosomal arrays using unmodified histones, indicating that the H2A N-terminus directly modulates the chromatin fiber likely through intra- and inter-nucleosomal arginine–DNA contacts to enable tighter nucleosomal packing.
evidence: Supported by in vitro experiments and structural analysis of nucleosome crystal structures.

claim: The H2A N-terminus is frequently mutated in cancer.
source: Our findings reveal a novel evolutionary mechanism for regulation of chromatin compaction and may explain the frequent mutations of the H2A N-terminus in cancer.
evidence: Supported by reference to COSMIC database showing 41 documented missense mutations in the H2A NTD.

claim: Nuclear volume has increased at a slower rate than genome size during eukaryotic evolution.
source: Within the same evolutionary timeframe, nuclear volume has also increased but at a slower rate than genome size expansion (Maul and Deaven, 1977; Olmo, 1982).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The ratio of nuclear to cell size has remained essentially constant in eukaryotes.
source: While the ratio of nuclear to cell size has remained essentially constant in eukaryotes (Cavalier-Smith, 2005), the disproportional increase in genome size relative to the nuclear volume has required organisms with larger genomes to compact their chromatin to greater extents than organisms with small sized genomes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Cavalier-Smith, 2005.

claim: Organisms with larger genomes must compact their chromatin to greater extents than organisms with small genomes.
source: While the ratio of nuclear to cell size has remained essentially constant in eukaryotes (Cavalier-Smith, 2005), the disproportional increase in genome size relative to the nuclear volume has required organisms with larger genomes to compact their chromatin to greater extents than organisms with small sized genomes.
evidence: Logical inference from the disproportionate increase in genome size relative to nuclear volume.

claim: There is a positive correlation between genome size and native chromatin compaction as measured by dye incorporation into chromatin.
source: Indeed there is a positive correlation between genome size and native chromatin compaction as measured by dye incorporation into chromatin (Vinogradov, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vinogradov, 2005.

claim: The genome is organized into chromatin by the repeating nucleosomal structure in most eukaryotes.
source: In most eukaryotes, the genome is organized into chromatin by the repeating nucleosomal structure (Luger et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Luger et al., 1997 and established scientific knowledge.

claim: Nucleosomes stack and fold into higher order structures to systematically compact the genome.
source: The nucleosomes stack and fold into higher order structures, serving to systematically compact the genome (Lieberman-Aiden et al., 2009; Duan et al., 2010) and to regulate molecular processes that are based on DNA (Celeste et al., 2002; Vogelauer et al., 2002; Fischle et al., 2005; Kouzarides, 2007; Fussner et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The surface of the histone octamer has 14 DNA interaction sites.
source: The surface of the histone octamer has 14 DNA interaction sites.
evidence: Supported by citation to Luger et al., 1997 in the following sentence.

claim: Each DNA interaction site on the histone octamer is mediated by an arginine residue that intercalates into the minor groove of the DNA.
source: Each interaction is mediated by an arginine residue that intercalates into the minor groove of the DNA to stabilize the nucleosomal structure (Luger et al., 1997; West et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Luger et al., 1997 and West et al., 2010.

claim: Arginine is the most commonly used amino acid for interaction with DNA.
source: Arginine is the most commonly used amino acid for interaction with DNA due to its positive charge and the lower energetic cost compared to lysine for displacing water when intercalating into the minor groove (Rohs et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rohs et al., 2009.

claim: Arginine has a lower energetic cost compared to lysine for displacing water when intercalating into the minor groove of DNA.
source: Arginine is the most commonly used amino acid for interaction with DNA due to its positive charge and the lower energetic cost compared to lysine for displacing water when intercalating into the minor groove (Rohs et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rohs et al., 2009.

claim: Nucleosomes form higher order structures through inter-nucleosomal contacts between the histone H4 N-terminal domain and the acidic patch of H2A.
source: For instance, nucleosomes form higher order structures through inter-nucleosomal contacts between the histone H4 N-terminal domain (NTD) and the acidic patch of H2A and between two H2B C-terminal domains (CTD) (Luger et al., 1997; Dorigo et al., 2003, 2004; Gordon et al., 2005; Schalch et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Nucleosomes form higher order structures through inter-nucleosomal contacts between two H2B C-terminal domains.
source: For instance, nucleosomes form higher order structures through inter-nucleosomal contacts between the histone H4 N-terminal domain (NTD) and the acidic patch of H2A and between two H2B C-terminal domains (CTD) (Luger et al., 1997; Dorigo et al., 2003, 2004; Gordon et al., 2005; Schalch et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Histone variants such as H2A.Z or H2A.Bbd can regulate the degree of chromatin compaction.
source: Histone variants, such as H2A.Z or H2A.Bbd, as well as post-translational modifications of histones, such as H4K16ac, can further regulate the degree of compaction (Suto et al., 2000; Bao et al., 2004; Shogren-Knaak et al., 2006; Zhou et al., 2007; Chandrasekharan et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2009; Fierz et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Post-translational modifications of histones such as H4K16ac can regulate the degree of chromatin compaction.
source: Histone variants, such as H2A.Z or H2A.Bbd, as well as post-translational modifications of histones, such as H4K16ac, can further regulate the degree of compaction (Suto et al., 2000; Bao et al., 2004; Shogren-Knaak et al., 2006; Zhou et al., 2007; Chandrasekharan et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2009; Fierz et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Polycomb complexes compact large domains of chromatin.
source: Polycomb complexes compact large domains of chromatin (Eskeland et al., 2010) and are important for proper development.
evidence: Supported by citation to Eskeland et al., 2010.

claim: Polycomb complexes are important for proper development.
source: Polycomb complexes compact large domains of chromatin (Eskeland et al., 2010) and are important for proper development.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Histones of the H1 family promote additional compaction by binding between nucleosomes to linker DNA near the DNA entry/exit site on nucleosomes.
source: Histones of the H1 family promote additional compaction by binding between nucleosomes to linker DNA near the DNA entry/exit site on nucleosomes and stabilize the intrinsic ability of nucleosomal arrays to fold in vitro (Carruthers et al., 1998; Robinson et al., 2008; Szerlong and Hansen, 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Linker histones stabilize the intrinsic ability of nucleosomal arrays to fold in vitro.
source: Histones of the H1 family promote additional compaction by binding between nucleosomes to linker DNA near the DNA entry/exit site on nucleosomes and stabilize the intrinsic ability of nucleosomal arrays to fold in vitro (Carruthers et al., 1998; Robinson et al., 2008; Szerlong and Hansen, 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Linker histones may affect chromatin compaction globally.
source: Linker histones may affect chromatin compaction globally (Fan et al., 2005), at specific stages of the cell cycle such as mitosis (Maresca et al., 2005) or at specific regions of the genome (Li et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fan et al., 2005.

claim: Linker histones may affect chromatin compaction at specific stages of the cell cycle such as mitosis.
source: Linker histones may affect chromatin compaction globally (Fan et al., 2005), at specific stages of the cell cycle such as mitosis (Maresca et al., 2005) or at specific regions of the genome (Li et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maresca et al., 2005.

claim: Linker histones may affect chromatin compaction at specific regions of the genome.
source: Linker histones may affect chromatin compaction globally (Fan et al., 2005), at specific stages of the cell cycle such as mitosis (Maresca et al., 2005) or at specific regions of the genome (Li et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2012.

claim: Linker histones are much less conserved than canonical histones.
source: In contrast to canonical histones, the linker histones are much less conserved (Caterino and Hayes, 2010), and ectopic expression of human linker histones in the budding yeast even at low levels is lethal for the cell (Miloshev et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Caterino and Hayes, 2010.

claim: Ectopic expression of human linker histones in budding yeast even at low levels is lethal for the cell.
source: In contrast to canonical histones, the linker histones are much less conserved (Caterino and Hayes, 2010), and ectopic expression of human linker histones in the budding yeast even at low levels is lethal for the cell (Miloshev et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Miloshev et al., 1994.

claim: Structural proteins such as condensin contribute to chromatin condensation.
source: Finally, structural proteins such as condensin also contribute to chromatin condensation (Tada et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tada et al., 2011.

claim: It has not been known whether the canonical histones themselves have evolved sequence features that contribute to increased chromatin compaction in organisms with larger genomes.
source: However, despite the existence of these mechanisms for genome compaction in higher eukaryotes, it has not been known whether the canonical histones themselves have evolved sequence features that also contribute to the generally increased chromatin compaction observed in organisms with larger genomes.
evidence: Statement of the knowledge gap that this study addresses.

claim: Of the canonical histones, the H2A NTD showed the most statistically significant variability in amino acid residues.
source: Of the canonical histones, the H2A NTD showed the most statistically significant variability in amino acid residues, where the number of arginines increased with increasing genome size (Figure 1A), while the number of serines (S) and threonines (T) decreased (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of 160 eukaryotic histone sequences and shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: The number of arginines in the H2A NTD increased with increasing genome size.
source: Of the canonical histones, the H2A NTD showed the most statistically significant variability in amino acid residues, where the number of arginines increased with increasing genome size (Figure 1A), while the number of serines (S) and threonines (T) decreased (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The number of serines and threonines in the H2A NTD decreased with increasing genome size.
source: Of the canonical histones, the H2A NTD showed the most statistically significant variability in amino acid residues, where the number of arginines increased with increasing genome size (Figure 1A), while the number of serines (S) and threonines (T) decreased (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Other amino acid residues in the H2A NTD, including lysines, did not correlate with genome size.
source: Other amino acid residues in the H2A NTD, including lysines (K), did not correlate with genome size (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The human H2A NTD contains arginine residues at positions 3 and 11 that are absent in yeast.
source: For instance, the human H2A NTD contains arginine residues at positions 3 and 11 that are absent in yeast and at position 20 which is correspondingly a lysine in yeast (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by sequence comparison shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The human H2A NTD contains an arginine at position 20 which is correspondingly a lysine in yeast.
source: For instance, the human H2A NTD contains arginine residues at positions 3 and 11 that are absent in yeast and at position 20 which is correspondingly a lysine in yeast (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by sequence comparison shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The human H2A NTD lacks S10 and S15 that are observed in the yeast H2A NTD.
source: In contrast, the human sequence lacks S10 and S15 that are observed in the yeast H2A NTD (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by sequence comparison shown in Figure 1C.

claim: At position 3, an arginine (R3) is predominantly present in medium and large species but is lacking in small species.
source: At position 3, an arginine (R3) is predominantly present in medium and large species but is lacking in small species.
evidence: Supported by heat map analysis in Figure 1D.

claim: At position 11, a lysine (K11) is observed in species with medium genomes that evolves to an arginine (R11) mainly in organisms with large genomes.
source: At position 11, a lysine (K11) is observed in species with medium genomes that evolves to an arginine (R11) mainly in organisms with large genomes.
evidence: Supported by heat map analysis in Figure 1D.

claim: R17 is present in most organisms examined, suggesting a very conserved function for this residue.
source: R17 is present in most organisms examined, suggesting a very conserved function for this residue (Zheng et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis and citation to Zheng et al., 2010.

claim: At position 20, small genomes contain predominantly a lysine residue, which converts to arginine in medium and large genomes.
source: At position 20, small genomes contain predominantly a lysine residue, which converts to arginine in medium and large genomes.
evidence: Supported by heat map analysis in Figure 1D.

claim: Serines/threonines at positions 10 and 15 are found primarily in organisms with small genomes and much less so in organisms with medium and large genomes.
source: In contrast, serines/threonines at positions 10 and 15 are found primarily in organisms with small genomes and much less so in organisms with medium and large genomes (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by heat map analysis in Figure 1D.

claim: Each of the four H2A NTD arginines is surrounded by a conserved motif.
source: Additionally, each of the four H2A NTD arginines is surrounded by a conserved motif (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The residues surrounding R3 and R17 are mainly glycine and serine, respectively.
source: The residues surrounding R3 and R17 are mainly glycine and serine, respectively.
evidence: Supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: At position 11, the motif varies based on genome size, with species with medium-sized genomes containing VKG and those with large genomes containing ARA.
source: At position 11, the motif varies based on genome size. Species with medium-sized genomes contain VKG and those with large genomes contain ARA.
evidence: Supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: At position 20, AKA is present in organisms with small genomes and (S/T)RA in larger genome species.
source: The same is true of position 20, where AKA is present in organisms with small genomes and (S/T)RA in larger genome species (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Except for R3, the positions of all the other evolutionarily varying residues in the H2A NTD are strongly conserved relative to the histone fold domain and not the N-terminus.
source: Interestingly, except for R3, the positions of all the other evolutionarily varying residues in the H2A NTD are strongly conserved relative to the histone fold domain and not the N-terminus (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by positional analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: R11, R17, and R20 are respectively 12, 6, and 3 amino acids away from the histone fold in most species.
source: However, these residues are respectively 12, 6, and 3 amino acids away from the histone fold in most species (note the vertical axes in Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by positional analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: S10 and S15 show more uniform positioning when counted from the histone fold.
source: S10 and S15—which are numbered based on the yeast sequence—also show more uniform positioning when counted from the histone fold.
evidence: Supported by positional analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Addition of a single arginine at position 3 (R3) to the H2A NTD was sufficient to significantly decrease the average interprobe distance by 18%.
source: When compared to the isogenic wild type (WT), addition of a single arginine at position 3 (R3) or 11 (R11) to the H2A NTD was sufficient to significantly decrease the average interprobe distance by 18% and 15%, respectively (Figure 2B,C; Table 1).
evidence: Supported by FISH experiments in yeast shown in Figure 2B,C and Table 1.

claim: Addition of a single arginine at position 11 (R11) to the H2A NTD was sufficient to significantly decrease the average interprobe distance by 15%.
source: When compared to the isogenic wild type (WT), addition of a single arginine at position 3 (R3) or 11 (R11) to the H2A NTD was sufficient to significantly decrease the average interprobe distance by 18% and 15%, respectively (Figure 2B,C; Table 1).
evidence: Supported by FISH experiments in yeast shown in Figure 2B,C and Table 1.

claim: The average interprobe distance was decreased by 22% when both R3 and R11 arginines were present (R3R11).
source: The average interprobe distance was further decreased by 22% when both arginines were present (R3R11) and even more so (30%) in R3(ΔGS10)R11.
evidence: Supported by FISH experiments in yeast shown in Table 1.

claim: The average interprobe distance was decreased by 30% in the R3(ΔGS10)R11 mutant.
source: The average interprobe distance was further decreased by 22% when both arginines were present (R3R11) and even more so (30%) in R3(ΔGS10)R11.
evidence: Supported by FISH experiments in yeast shown in Table 1.

claim: Deleting G9S10 (ΔGS10) alone caused slightly increased compaction with low statistical significance.
source: Deleting G9S10 (ΔGS10) alone caused slightly increased compaction with low statistical significance (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by FISH experiments in yeast shown in Table 1.

claim: The largest decrease in interprobe distance (41%) was observed in the R11ΔS15 mutant.
source: The largest decrease in interprobe distance (41%) was observed in the R11ΔS15 mutant, which places R11 12 amino acids from the histone fold, the same position as in organisms with large genomes.
evidence: Supported by FISH experiments in yeast shown in Table 1.

claim: The R11ΔS15 mutant places R11 12 amino acids from the histone fold, the same position as in organisms with large genomes.
source: The largest decrease in interprobe distance (41%) was observed in the R11ΔS15 mutant, which places R11 12 amino acids from the histone fold, the same position as in organisms with large genomes.
evidence: Based on the design of the mutant and sequence analysis.

claim: Removal of S15 (ΔS15) alone had no effect on interprobe distance.
source: Removal of S15 (ΔS15) alone had no effect.
evidence: Supported by FISH experiments in yeast shown in Table 1.

claim: Insertions of lysines at positions 3 and 11 did not significantly affect the interprobe distances.
source: The effect of arginines was not simply due to increasing the positive charge of the H2A NTD, as insertions of lysines at positions 3 and 11 did not significantly affect the interprobe distances (Figure 2C and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by FISH experiments in yeast shown in Figure 2C and Supplementary file 2.

claim: R17K or K20R mutations did not affect compaction.
source: Additionally, R17K or K20R mutations did not affect compaction, nor did a randomly inserted arginine at position 6 (R6) (Figure 2C and Supplementary file 2), suggesting that not every arginine in the H2A NTD contributes to chromatin compaction.
evidence: Supported by FISH experiments in yeast shown in Figure 2C and Supplementary file 2.

claim: A randomly inserted arginine at position 6 (R6) did not affect compaction.
source: Additionally, R17K or K20R mutations did not affect compaction, nor did a randomly inserted arginine at position 6 (R6) (Figure 2C and Supplementary file 2), suggesting that not every arginine in the H2A NTD contributes to chromatin compaction.
evidence: Supported by FISH experiments in yeast shown in Figure 2C and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Not every arginine in the H2A NTD contributes to chromatin compaction.
source: Additionally, R17K or K20R mutations did not affect compaction, nor did a randomly inserted arginine at position 6 (R6) (Figure 2C and Supplementary file 2), suggesting that not every arginine in the H2A NTD contributes to chromatin compaction.
evidence: Inference from the experimental data showing that R6 does not affect compaction.

claim: The interprobe distances for all probe sets were significantly decreased in R11 compared to WT.
source: The interprobe distances for all probe sets were significantly decreased in R11 compared to WT and even more so in R11ΔS15 but not ΔS15 alone (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by FISH experiments with multiple probe sets shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: The interprobe distances for all probe sets were even more decreased in R11ΔS15 compared to WT.
source: The interprobe distances for all probe sets were significantly decreased in R11 compared to WT and even more so in R11ΔS15 but not ΔS15 alone (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by FISH experiments with multiple probe sets shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: ΔS15 alone did not significantly decrease interprobe distances.
source: The interprobe distances for all probe sets were significantly decreased in R11 compared to WT and even more so in R11ΔS15 but not ΔS15 alone (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by FISH experiments with multiple probe sets shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: R11 causes uniform compaction across large genomic distances.
source: Plotting the physical vs genomic distances for all probe sets revealed uniform compaction across large genomic distances (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by analysis of multiple probe sets shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The effect of R11 on chromatin compaction was not strain-specific.
source: The effect of R11 on chromatin compaction was not strain-specific as H2A R11 and R11ΔS15, but not ΔS15, caused chromatin compaction in a different strain background (Figure 2E; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by FISH experiments in a different yeast strain background shown in Figure 2E.

claim: There are essentially no differences in nucleosomal density in H2A arginine mutants using Micrococcal nuclease (MNase) digestion.
source: We find that there are essentially no differences in nucleosomal density in H2A arginine mutants using Micrococcal nuclease (MNase) digestion (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), indicating that the average nucleosomal spacing is not affected by these mutations.
evidence: Supported by MNase digestion experiments shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The average nucleosomal spacing is not affected by H2A arginine mutations.
source: We find that there are essentially no differences in nucleosomal density in H2A arginine mutants using Micrococcal nuclease (MNase) digestion (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), indicating that the average nucleosomal spacing is not affected by these mutations.
evidence: Inference from MNase digestion data showing no differences in nucleosomal density.

claim: The more compact mutants displayed decreased accessibility to MNase as indicated by the delayed appearance of the nucleosomal digestion pattern.
source: But the more compact mutants displayed decreased accessibility to MNase as indicated by the delayed appearance of the nucleosomal digestion pattern (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by MNase digestion experiments shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: H2A mutants containing R11 or R3R11 displayed significantly decreased nuclear volumes compared to WT cells.
source: As compared to WT cells, H2A mutants containing R11 or R3R11, both of which contain more compact chromatin, displayed significantly decreased nuclear volumes.
evidence: Supported by nuclear volume measurements shown in Figure 3B and Table 1.

claim: The average nuclear volume in the R3 mutant was less than WT but did not reach statistical significance.
source: The average nuclear volume in the R3 mutant was also less than WT but did not reach statistical significance.
evidence: Supported by nuclear volume measurements shown in Figure 3B and Table 1.

claim: H2A mutants from which serines 10 and 15 were removed displayed larger nuclear volumes.
source: Interestingly, H2A mutants from which serines 10 and 15 were removed displayed larger nuclear volumes.
evidence: Supported by nuclear volume measurements shown in Figure 3B and Table 1.

claim: Simultaneous insertions of arginines into ΔGS10 and ΔS15 strains (R3(ΔGS10)R11 and R11ΔS15) decreased their nuclear volume, restoring them to levels similar to WT.
source: Simultaneous insertions of arginines into these strains (R3(ΔGS10)R11 and R11ΔS15) decreased their nuclear volume (R11ΔS15 p<0.001 compared to ΔS15), restoring them to levels similar to WT.
evidence: Supported by nuclear volume measurements shown in Figure 3B and Table 1.

claim: The control strains with either lysines or R6 had nuclear volumes similar to or larger than WT.
source: The control strains with either lysines or R6 had nuclear volumes similar to or larger than WT.
evidence: Supported by nuclear volume measurements shown in Figure 3B and Table 1.

claim: Neither arginines nor serines had any effect on total cell size as measured by concanavalin A staining.
source: Neither arginines nor serines had any effect on total cell size as measured by concanavalin A staining (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by cell volume measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: In the FY406 strain background, ΔS15 did not cause an increase in nuclear volume.
source: In the FY406 strain background, ΔS15 did not cause an increase in nuclear volume; and thus both R11 and R11ΔS15 strains exhibited smaller nuclear volumes than isogenic WT (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by nuclear volume measurements in FY406 background shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Both R11 and R11ΔS15 strains exhibited smaller nuclear volumes than isogenic WT in the FY406 strain background.
source: In the FY406 strain background, ΔS15 did not cause an increase in nuclear volume; and thus both R11 and R11ΔS15 strains exhibited smaller nuclear volumes than isogenic WT (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by nuclear volume measurements in FY406 background shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Modulation of chromatin compaction through the H2A NTD, especially in the presence of R11, affects the nuclear volume.
source: These data suggest that modulation of chromatin compaction through the H2A NTD, especially in the presence of R11, affects the nuclear volume but this effect may be indirect (see human data below).
evidence: Inference from the nuclear volume data in yeast.

claim: Cells overexpressing ΔR3, R11A, or ΔR3R11A H2A mutants had increased interprobe distances, indicating de-compaction of chromatin.
source: Cells overexpressing ΔR3, R11A, or ΔR3R11A H2A mutants had increased interprobe distances, indicating de-compaction of chromatin.
evidence: Supported by FISH experiments in human cells shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Expression of H2A R11K had modest effects on chromatin de-compaction with marginal statistical significance.
source: Expression of H2A R11K had modest effects on chromatin de-compaction with marginal statistical significance (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by FISH experiments in human cells shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Cells expressing any of the H2A mutants (ΔR3, R11A, R11K, ΔR3R11A) displayed larger nuclear areas.
source: Cells expressing any of the H2A mutants displayed larger nuclear areas, suggesting that nuclear size is increased (Figure 4C,D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–F; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by nuclear area measurements in human cells shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Ectopic expression of a C-terminally FLAG-tagged H2A mutant missing residues 1–12 (Δ1–12) caused significant de-compaction of chromatin.
source: Ectopic expression of a C-terminally FLAG-tagged H2A mutant missing residues 1–12 (Δ1–12) also caused significant de-compaction of chromatin and increased nuclear area despite being expressed at a lower level than WT (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: Supported by FISH experiments in human cells shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Ectopic expression of H2A Δ1–12 caused increased nuclear area despite being expressed at a lower level than WT.
source: Ectopic expression of a C-terminally FLAG-tagged H2A mutant missing residues 1–12 (Δ1–12) also caused significant de-compaction of chromatin and increased nuclear area despite being expressed at a lower level than WT (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: Supported by nuclear area measurements and expression analysis in human cells shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: The H2A NTD, especially arginines 3 and 11, function to compact chromatin in human cells.
source: These data demonstrate that, consistent with our predictions, the H2A NTD, especially arginines 3 and 11, function to compact chromatin in human cells.
evidence: Inference from the human cell experiments showing de-compaction when arginines are removed.

claim: Arrays containing WT H2A sedimented with a coefficient of 33.1 in the absence of Mg2+.
source: In the absence of Mg2+, arrays containing WT H2A sedimented with a coefficient of 33.1, which is a value that has been previously shown for similar arrays (Dorigo et al., 2003; Shogren-Knaak et al., 2006; Zhou et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by analytical ultracentrifugation experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Arrays missing R11 adopted a more extended conformation with a smaller sedimentation coefficient of 31.0 in the absence of Mg2+.
source: In contrast, arrays missing R11 adopted a more extended conformation with a smaller sedimentation coefficient of 31.0 (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by analytical ultracentrifugation experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Addition of Mg2+ increased compaction of both WT and ΔR11 arrays and shifted the sedimentation coefficients to 39.3 and 37.4, respectively.
source: Addition of Mg2+ increased compaction of both arrays and shifted the sedimentation coefficients to 39.3 and 37.4 for WT and ΔR11 H2A, respectively (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by analytical ultracentrifugation experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the absence of R11 in the H2A NTD, nucleosomal arrays adopt a less compact conformation even in the presence of divalent cations.
source: Thus, in the absence of R11 in the H2A NTD, nucleosomal arrays adopt a less compact conformation even in the presence of divalent cations, showing that R11 directly increases chromatin compaction.
evidence: Inference from the analytical ultracentrifugation data showing lower sedimentation coefficients for ΔR11 arrays.

claim: R11 directly increases chromatin compaction.
source: Thus, in the absence of R11 in the H2A NTD, nucleosomal arrays adopt a less compact conformation even in the presence of divalent cations, showing that R11 directly increases chromatin compaction.
evidence: Inference from in vitro experiments showing that R11 affects compaction in the absence of other cellular factors.

claim: There was a high level of correlation (≥0.99) between all yeast strains examined for gene expression.
source: Remarkably, there was a high level of correlation (≥0.99) between all strains examined (Figure 6A), and no specific gene ontology was found among the genes that were differentially expressed by twofold or more.
evidence: Supported by gene expression microarray analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: No specific gene ontology was found among the genes that were differentially expressed by twofold or more in H2A mutants.
source: Remarkably, there was a high level of correlation (≥0.99) between all strains examined (Figure 6A), and no specific gene ontology was found among the genes that were differentially expressed by twofold or more.
evidence: Supported by gene expression microarray analysis.

claim: The expression levels of the histone genes were similar across H2A mutants.
source: The expression levels of the histone genes were similar, indicating that altered levels of histone genes expression do not account for the changes in chromatin compaction.
evidence: Supported by gene expression microarray analysis.

claim: Altered levels of histone genes expression do not account for the changes in chromatin compaction in H2A mutants.
source: The expression levels of the histone genes were similar, indicating that altered levels of histone genes expression do not account for the changes in chromatin compaction.
evidence: Inference from the observation that histone gene expression is similar across mutants.

claim: Compaction of chromatin by H2A does not significantly alter global gene expression in exponentially growing cells.
source: These data indicate that compaction of chromatin by H2A does not significantly alter global gene expression in exponentially growing cells.
evidence: Inference from the high correlation in gene expression between WT and H2A mutants.

claim: All H2A mutant strains showed similar growth rates in rich media.
source: All strains also showed similar growth rates in rich media (Figure 6B) and no significant differences in sensitivity to hydroxyurea, methyl methanesulfonate (MMS), bleomycin, 4-nitroquinoline 1-oxide (4NQO), cycloheximide, and rapamycin, indicating no major defects with DNA replication or repair, protein synthesis, or the TOR signaling pathways (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by growth curve analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: H2A mutant strains showed no significant differences in sensitivity to hydroxyurea, MMS, bleomycin, 4NQO, cycloheximide, and rapamycin.
source: All strains also showed similar growth rates in rich media (Figure 6B) and no significant differences in sensitivity to hydroxyurea, methyl methanesulfonate (MMS), bleomycin, 4-nitroquinoline 1-oxide (4NQO), cycloheximide, and rapamycin, indicating no major defects with DNA replication or repair, protein synthesis, or the TOR signaling pathways (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by spot test analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: H2A mutant strains have no major defects with DNA replication or repair, protein synthesis, or the TOR signaling pathways.
source: All strains also showed similar growth rates in rich media (Figure 6B) and no significant differences in sensitivity to hydroxyurea, methyl methanesulfonate (MMS), bleomycin, 4-nitroquinoline 1-oxide (4NQO), cycloheximide, and rapamycin, indicating no major defects with DNA replication or repair, protein synthesis, or the TOR signaling pathways (Figure 6C).
evidence: Inference from the lack of sensitivity to various drugs that target these pathways.

claim: In competition growth assays, the H2A mutants regardless of any effect on chromatin compaction were outcompeted by WT.
source: But in competition growth assays in which equal amounts of WT and H2A mutant cells harboring the PGK1 gene fused to either GFP or RFP were co-cultured, the H2A mutants regardless of any effect on chromatin compaction, were outcompeted (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Changes in the H2A NTD sequence can affect the overall fitness of the cell.
source: This suggests that changes in the H2A NTD sequence can affect the overall fitness of the cell.
evidence: Inference from the competition assay showing that H2A mutants are outcompeted.

claim: A survey of the COSMIC database revealed 41 documented missense mutations within the H2A NTD.
source: A survey of the COSMIC database (Forbes et al., 2011), as of the time of writing, revealed 41 documented missense mutations within the H2A NTD with 29 (71%) affecting a residue within one of the four arginine motifs (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by analysis of the COSMIC database.

claim: 29 (71%) of the documented H2A NTD mutations in cancer affect a residue within one of the four arginine motifs.
source: A survey of the COSMIC database (Forbes et al., 2011), as of the time of writing, revealed 41 documented missense mutations within the H2A NTD with 29 (71%) affecting a residue within one of the four arginine motifs (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by analysis of the COSMIC database shown in Figure 7A.

claim: R11 is the most commonly mutated residue in the H2A NTD in cancer.
source: R11, which had the strongest effect of any single arginine residue on chromatin compaction, is the most commonly mutated residue in the H2A NTD.
evidence: Supported by analysis of the COSMIC database shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Ectopic expression of R11C, R11H, and R11P in normal human fibroblasts decreases chromatin compaction significantly.
source: We tested the effects of three of these mutations, R11C, H, and P and found that ectopic expression of each in normal human fibroblasts decreases chromatin compaction significantly with R11P having the strongest effect (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: Supported by FISH experiments in human cells shown in Figure 7B,C.

claim: R11P has the strongest effect on decreasing chromatin compaction among the cancer mutations tested.
source: We tested the effects of three of these mutations, R11C, H, and P and found that ectopic expression of each in normal human fibroblasts decreases chromatin compaction significantly with R11P having the strongest effect (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: Supported by FISH experiments in human cells shown in Figure 7B,C.

claim: Cancer mutations R11C, R11H, and R11P have little effect on increasing nuclear area.
source: These cancer mutations have little effect on increasing nuclear area, however (Figure 7D,E), in contrast to R11A (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by nuclear area measurements in human cells shown in Figure 7D,E.

claim: Over-expression of an H2A mutant has the potential to disrupt chromatin compaction in cancer.
source: But our data suggest that over-expression of an H2A mutant has the potential to disrupt chromatin compaction in cancer.
evidence: Inference from the experiments showing that overexpressed H2A mutants affect chromatin compaction.

claim: R3 is at 2.87 Å from the DNA and could potentially bind the DNA gyre as the DNA wraps around the histone octamer.
source: R3 is at 2.87 Å from the DNA and could potentially bind the DNA gyre as the DNA wraps around the histone octamer.
evidence: Supported by analysis of crystal structure data from Davey et al., 2002.

claim: R11 forms close contacts with the DNA phosphate backbone of self and neighboring nucleosomes (4.09, 2.90 Å, respectively).
source: R11 forms close contacts with the DNA phosphate backbone of self and neighboring nucleosomes (4.09, 2.90 Å, respectively).
evidence: Supported by analysis of crystal structure data from Davey et al., 2002.

claim: The evolutionary appearance of arginines in the H2A NTD sequence at positions 3 and 11 corresponds to strategic positioning of R3 and R11 within the nucleosome structure that may enable interactions with the DNA.
source: Thus, the evolutionary appearance of arginines in the H2A NTD sequence at positions 3 and 11 corresponds to strategic positioning of R3 and R11 within the nucleosome structure that may enable interactions with the DNA, leading to more compact chromatin.
evidence: Inference from structural analysis and evolutionary data.

claim: The mechanism of interprobe distance shortening in the presence of H2A arginines R3 and R11 is likely due to increased linear compaction rather than increased chromatin looping.
source: While the mechanism of this shortening is still unknown, the two most likely explanations are due to linear chromosomal compaction or increased chromatin looping (Bohn and Heermann, 2010). However, our data are more consistent with increased linear compaction due to several reasons.
evidence: Inference from multiple lines of evidence including uniform compaction across probe pairs, de-compaction in human cells, and in vitro data.

claim: The intra- and inter-nucleosomal interactions between arginines and DNA may serve to neutralize the negative charge of the DNA backbone, leading to enhanced stacking of nucleosomes.
source: These intra- and inter-nucleosomal interactions with the arginines and the DNA may serve to neutralize the negative charge of the DNA backbone, leading to enhanced stacking of nucleosomes and hence increased compaction.
evidence: Speculative mechanism based on structural analysis and experimental data.

claim: R17 and R20 do not affect compaction by themselves because they are more buried from the surface.
source: Consistent with this model, the other two arginine residues in the H2A NTD, R17 and R20, which are more buried from the surface, do not affect compaction by themselves.
evidence: Inference from structural analysis and experimental data showing no effect of R17K or K20R mutations.

claim: The functions of R17 and R20 may be to modulate the effects of the surrounding residues.
source: However, their functions may be to modulate the effects of the surrounding residues.
evidence: Speculation about the potential roles of R17 and R20.

claim: The cell may be able to dynamically regulate chromatin compaction by H2A arginines through posttranslational modifications.
source: Although all canonical H2A genes contain R3 and R11 in humans, the cell may still be able to dynamically regulate chromatin compaction by these arginines. For instance, arginines may be subject to posttranslational modifications, such a methylation which makes the arginine residue bulkier, or citrullination which removes the positive charge (Wang et al., 2001; Hagiwara et al., 2005; Di Lorenzo and Bedford, 2011; Waldmann et al., 2011).
evidence: Speculation supported by citations to prior work on arginine modifications.

claim: The H2A NTD is situated in close proximity to the H2B CTD which when ubiquitylated, disrupts chromatin compaction in vitro.
source: Interestingly, the H2A NTD is situated in close proximity to the H2B CTD which when ubiquitylated, disrupts chromatin compaction in vitro (Fierz et al., 2011), lending support to the ability of this region of the nucleosome to modulate chromatin compaction.
evidence: Supported by citation to Fierz et al., 2011.

claim: The inability of lysines, especially at position 11, to increase chromatin compaction suggests exquisite structural constraints for H2A-mediated chromatin compaction.
source: The inability of lysines, especially at position 11, to increase chromatin compaction suggests exquisite structural constraints for H2A-mediated chromatin compaction.
evidence: Inference from the experimental data showing that lysines do not have the same effect as arginines.

claim: Additional amino acid changes would be required for lysines in the H2A NTD to increase genome compaction.
source: So, it is conceivable that additional amino acid changes would be required for lysines in the H2A NTD to increase genome compaction.
evidence: Speculation based on the observation that lysines in different contexts may have different effects.

claim: The nucleoskeletal theory proposes that chromatin structure influences the shape of the nucleus and is a major determinant of nuclear volume.
source: The nucleoskeletal theory proposes that chromatin structure influences the shape of the nucleus, and thus is a major determinant of nuclear volume (Cavalier-Smith, 2005), although the amount of DNA per se does not affect nuclear volume (Neumann and Nurse, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cavalier-Smith, 2005 and Neumann and Nurse, 2007.

claim: The amount of DNA per se does not affect nuclear volume.
source: The nucleoskeletal theory proposes that chromatin structure influences the shape of the nucleus, and thus is a major determinant of nuclear volume (Cavalier-Smith, 2005), although the amount of DNA per se does not affect nuclear volume (Neumann and Nurse, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Neumann and Nurse, 2007.

claim: Non-chromatin components such as nuclear import factors from the cytoplasm may also modulate nuclear size.
source: Non-chromatin components such as nuclear import factors from the cytoplasm may also modulate nuclear size (Levy and Heald, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Levy and Heald, 2010.

claim: There is not a clear-cut relationship between nuclear volume and chromatin compaction in H2A mutants.
source: Although we do not observe a clear-cut relationship between nuclear volume and chromatin compaction, our data identify a region of the nucleosome that is directly or indirectly linked to nuclear volume control mechanisms.
evidence: Inference from the complex relationship between compaction and nuclear volume observed in the data.

claim: The H2A NTD is a region of the nucleosome that is directly or indirectly linked to nuclear volume control mechanisms.
source: Although we do not observe a clear-cut relationship between nuclear volume and chromatin compaction, our data identify a region of the nucleosome that is directly or indirectly linked to nuclear volume control mechanisms.
evidence: Inference from the data showing effects of H2A NTD mutations on nuclear volume.

claim: H2A-mediated compaction of chromatin may have evolved as a mechanism to enable regulation of chromatin compaction without having to make compensatory changes to all other processes that are also based on DNA such as transcription.
source: These data raise the possibility that H2A-mediated compaction of chromatin may have evolved as a mechanism to enable regulation of chromatin compaction without having to make compensatory changes to all other processes that are also based on DNA such as transcription.
evidence: Speculation based on the observation that H2A mutations affect compaction but not gene expression.

claim: Organisms with small genomes but very small cell size may face similar physical constraints as those with larger genomes and may use arginine-containing H2A as a means for chromatin compaction.
source: Organisms with small genomes but also very small cell size may face similar physical constraints as those with larger genomes, and may therefore use arginine-containing H2A as a means for chromatin compaction.
evidence: Speculation based on the example of Ostreococcus tauri.

claim: Ostreococcus tauri possesses an R3-containing H2A and is a free-living unicellular algae with a very small genome of 12.6 Mbp and a cell diameter of 0.8 µm.
source: For instance, Ostreococcus tauri which possesses an R3-containing H2A, is a free-living unicellular algae that has a very small genome of 12.6 Mbp but a cell diameter of 0.8 µm (Palenik et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Palenik et al., 2007.

claim: S. cerevisiae has a similarly sized genome to Ostreococcus tauri but has a cell diameter that is approximately five times larger.
source: S. cerevisiae, which does not contain an H2A with R3, has a similarly sized genome but has a cell diameter that is approximately five times larger.
evidence: Comparison based on known genome sizes and cell dimensions.

claim: Certain organisms such as Oikopleura dioica have distinctive life cycles and possess H2A genes with and without arginines, which may enable them to dynamically regulate genome compaction at different stages of their life cycles.
source: Furthermore, certain organisms such as Oikopleura dioica, which has one of the smallest genomes in animals, have distinctive life cycles and possess H2A genes with and without arginines, which may enable them to dynamically regulate genome compaction at different stages of their life cycles (Moosmann et al., 2011) (for species with H2A isoforms, see attached spreadsheet).
evidence: Speculation supported by citation to Moosmann et al., 2011.

claim: The H2A arginines may have evolved in circumstances when the genome size became disproportionately large compared to nuclear volume.
source: So, the H2A arginines may have evolved in circumstances when the genome size became disproportionately large compared to nuclear volume.
evidence: Inference from the evolutionary analysis and examples provided.

claim: The toad Bufo gargarizans has a genome size that is twice as large as the human genome and possesses an H2A gene with R3, R11, and glutamine 6 replaced with an arginine.
source: Interestingly, the toad, Bufo gargarizans, which has a genome size that is twice as large as the human genome, possesses an H2A gene with not only R3 and R11 but also glutamine 6 replaced with an arginine, suggesting that additional arginines in the H2A tail may enable further compaction in organisms with even larger genomes.
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis of Bufo gargarizans H2A.

claim: Additional arginines in the H2A tail may enable further compaction in organisms with even larger genomes.
source: Interestingly, the toad, Bufo gargarizans, which has a genome size that is twice as large as the human genome, possesses an H2A gene with not only R3 and R11 but also glutamine 6 replaced with an arginine, suggesting that additional arginines in the H2A tail may enable further compaction in organisms with even larger genomes.
evidence: Speculation based on the observation of additional arginines in Bufo gargarizans H2A.

claim: Deregulated chromatin compaction is often a pathological hallmark of cancer cells.
source: Deregulated chromatin compaction is often a pathological hallmark of cancer cells (Edens et al., 2012), although the underlying mechanisms are not well-understood.
evidence: Supported by citation to Edens et al., 2012.

claim: The reported mutations in the histone H2A NTD may contribute to the altered chromatin compaction that is commonly observed in cancer cells.
source: Our findings also suggest that the reported mutations in the histone H2A NTD may contribute to the altered chromatin compaction that is commonly observed in cancer cells (Zink et al., 2004).
evidence: Speculation based on the findings that H2A NTD mutations affect compaction and are found in cancer.
